pages.title: Customer retention | Firstsource Glossary
pages.text: ## Why it matters The economics consistently favor retention over acquisition, and by a wide enough margin that most companies' actual budget allocation looks misaligned with the data. Existing customers also convert at dramatically higher rates and spend more per transaction, which compounds the case for treating retention as a primary growth lever rather than a secondary defensive metric. The headline figures make the point. Acquiring a new customer costs 5 to 25 times more than retaining an existing one, and a 5% improvement in customer retention can boost profits by 25% to 95%, yet only about 18% of companies focus more on retention than acquisition. That gap between what the data supports and where budgets go is the opportunity. [...] Because the cost of acquiring a replacement customer is so much higher than the cost of keeping an existing one that even a modest reduction in churn compounds significantly over time: fewer replacement acquisitions needed, more cumulative lifetime revenue per retained customer, and lower servicing costs for customers who've been with a company longer and require less onboarding support. ### What is a save desk and how does it fit into customer retention? A save desk is a specialized team or workflow focused specifically on engaging customers who've signaled intent to cancel, typically equipped with retention-specific offers and greater discretion than a standard service agent, precisely because this moment carries outsized impact on the retention rate.

analysis.answer: A 2005 paper in the Journal of Targeting, Measurement and Analysis for Marketing says it is often claimed that acquiring a new customer costs five times as much as retaining an existing one [1]. The same paper examines whether that 5X ratio should lead firms to spend more on retention, and finds that under the Blattberg and Deighton model the answer depends on whether the costs are average or marginal [1]. If the 5X ratio refers to average costs, the paper says it does not necessarily imply that a firm should spend more on retention [1]. The available excerpts do not establish that acquiring a customer actually costs 5 times more than retaining one; the 5X figure is presented as a common saying, and the other page's provided text does not address it [1] [2].
